strengths: The paper addresses a practical stitching problem: locally repairing alignment errors that seam selection alone cannot avoid. Figures 1, 10, and 11 show convincing improvements to structures such as curbs, paving, and stairs.

The pipeline is intuitive and potentially useful as an addition to existing stitching systems. Constraining local seam labels at patch boundaries provides a sensible mechanism for reconnecting repaired regions to the original seam.

Experiments cover 79 image pairs across three datasets. Reported seam errors generally improve over methods [16,17], and runtime comparisons show substantial savings over iterative method [17]. The 20-participant study gives the proposed method 108 of 160 first-place votes on the selected examples.

The manuscript clearly attributes its principal components and public datasets, reports key parameter settings and hardware, and includes a useful failure example and candid discussion of its dependence on initial alignment.
weaknesses: The incremental contribution is insufficiently isolated experimentally. SSIM-based seam evaluation comes from [17], correspondence estimation uses SIFT flow, and the main additions are selective patch repair and flow tapering. Beyond the single example in Figure 4, there are no systematic ablations establishing the benefits of component selection, sigmoid tapering versus simpler weighting, or seam reconnection. Testing only one initial alignment and seam-cutting combination also leaves the claimed general applicability unverified.

Evidence for perceptual superiority is limited. Equation (5) evaluates essentially the same SSIM discrepancy used to select repairs and does not independently assess deformation, duplicated content, or artifacts away from the seam. The authors themselves identify a disagreement between this metric and visual quality. The user study provides complementary evidence, but its eight manually selected 'controversial' examples, without reported presentation randomization, per-scene results, or uncertainty, do not establish general perceptual improvement.

Quantitative comparisons include only seam-cutting methods [16,17], which retain the initial alignment. Comparisons with seam-driven methods [18,26] are restricted to selected visual results, and relevant cited alternatives such as the large-parallax method [12] are not evaluated. The experiments therefore establish the benefit of adding local alignment more clearly than its advantage over competing parallax-tolerant stitching approaches.

The central flow modification is underspecified. Section 3.4 writes the modified displacement as f(V(p)), but Equation (4) defines a scalar sigmoid whose argument is normalized spatial position. The actual vector scaling rule, orientation selection, treatment of other patch boundaries, and handling of overlapping repair patches need clarification for reproducibility.

The claim that the method can 'almost remove' the rough-alignment assumption exceeds the demonstrated scope. Section 3.4 assumes small residual parallax within extracted patches, and Section 3.3 declares a seam plausible when max(Q) <= 1.5 mean(Q), which also accepts uniformly high errors. The limitations discussion appropriately acknowledges widespread misalignment, but no controlled evaluation establishes the range of displacement or initial-alignment quality the method can tolerate.
